About

Weather, science, and the people who use forecasts

I am a meteorologist and PhD candidate at Brown University, where I work with Professor Amanda Lynch. My research focuses on Arctic storms, particularly polar lows, and on understanding their development through numerical weather modeling and observational analysis.

My work also includes machine learning for sea ice applications and the relationship between severe weather and maritime safety.

Before beginning my PhD, I worked in operational weather forecasting in Brazil and researched subseasonal precipitation prediction. Those experiences continue to shape my interest in connecting atmospheric science with decisions that people make in hazardous weather.

I am visiting the Norwegian Meteorological Institute in Oslo from October through December 2026, learning more about weather forecasting and the communication of hazards in the Nordic Seas.

Research

What I work on

My research combines atmospheric dynamics, numerical models, and environmental data to study weather and climate in high latitudes.

Atmospheric dynamics

Polar lows and Arctic storms

Using Polar WRF experiments to examine how sea ice, topography, surface fluxes, and storm processes affect the development and intensity of polar lows.

Storm development

Marine cold air outbreaks

Investigating how exposure to marine cold air outbreak conditions influences polar low development and why individual storms respond differently.

Machine learning

Sea ice and high resolution information

Applying generative adversarial networks to enhance sea ice concentration resolution in a strait along the Northern Sea Route.

Weather hazards

Arctic maritime safety

Examining severe weather hazards such as polar lows and ship icing, and their relevance for people operating in Arctic waters.

Forecast evaluation

Precipitation in Brazil

Evaluating subseasonal precipitation simulations in Brazil's São Francisco River Basin using the Eta model.

Research & practice

Forecast use and communication

Connecting modeling research with operational forecasting, public communication, and the practical interpretation of weather risks.
